Problem note

Paths in Polynomial Lemniscates:\\A Degree-Seven Counterexample\\and Two Short-Path Criteria

Erdős #1041 28 pp By Will Cook 23 September 2026
PDFOpen the PDF · 28 pp TeXLaTeX source Source on GitHub Problem dossier

Précis

For a monic trinomial 𝑓(𝑧) =𝑧𝑛 +𝑎𝑧𝑚 +𝑏,1 ≤𝑚 <𝑛f(z)=zn+azm+b,1≤m<n, with roots in the open unit disc, the root equation controls f on every root-to-origin segment. Any two distinct roots are consequently joined inside {|f|<1} by an explicit two-segment path of length less than 2. Abel summation explains the role of the missing coefficients, and a sextic example shows why root locations alone do not control these segments. A squarefree monic polynomial has such a contained path when its least critical-value modulus is at most 13/2513/25, without a root-location hypothesis; a scale-free consequence completes the main note. Independent estimates and limitations of other constructions are collected in the supplementary sections.

This paper owns the problem-specific exposition for Erdős #1041: ordinary all-degree trinomial paths, bounded-radius concyclic chords, a sharp critical-value mean, subsidiary Lean and Comparator checks, and exact obstructions that prevent promoting those estimates to a general connector theorem.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or the current status of Erdős #1041, including the later one-polynomial Formal Conjectures path-image Hausdorff-length check and its unreviewed historical curve-length correspondence; those distinctions belong to docs/claims.json in the mathematics repository.

Authorship and AI use. Will Cook built and directed the research infrastructure and maintains the public release. He reviewed claims when he could. AI agents did most of the research and drafting. Cook did not independently verify every claim.

Cite and contact. Cite this paper by its title, author and date above, with its PDF; cite the earlier sources it uses for a mathematical result. For software, use the release citation and give the commit used. Contact Will with questions or corrections.

The question and a degree-seven counterexample

Problem 1.1 (Erdős #1041). Let 𝑓(𝑧) =∏𝑛𝑖=1(𝑧 −𝑧𝑖)f(z)=∏i=1n(z−zi) be monic with 𝑛 ≥2n≥2 and all 𝑧𝑖zi in the open unit disc. Must two root occurrences be joined by a curve of length less than 22 inside {|𝑓| <1}{|f|<1}?

Repeated roots give a constant path between two listed occurrences, so the geometric question concerns squarefree polynomials. The original question is Problem 5 of Erdős–Herzog–Piranian [2], listed as Problem 1041 in Bloom’s catalogue [1]. Pendyala [4] proves the complete degree-four case by a close-pair chord or two radial segments through the centre of a smallest enclosing disc. That centre need not be a critical point. The results here concern specified polynomial families and sufficient conditions; no priority claim is made.

The degree-seven polynomial constructed by erdosproblems.com contributor ani has distinct roots in the open unit disc. Lean proves that every preconnected subset of its strict unit lemniscate containing two distinct roots has one-dimensional Hausdorff measure greater than 22. In particular, the image of every continuous root-to-root path has this measure, and Lean proves the negation and answer(False) forms of the exact Formal Conjectures statement.1

The next two sections give sufficient conditions under which two roots are joined by a short path. Each is a hypothesis on 𝑓f, and neither applies to the polynomial of ani: it has eight nonzero coefficients, and all its critical values lie very near the unit circle. Section 2 treats trinomials; its proof prescribes a path for every pair of distinct roots. Section 3 requires the least critical-value modulus to be at most 13/2513/25, imposes no coefficient pattern or root-location hypothesis, and selects some pair of roots. The supplementary sections retain the other estimates and the obstructions to prescribed constructions.

Links in the running text go to Lean proofs of single steps, such as a finite inequality; such a link does not cover the surrounding argument. No independent review of the analytic arguments is recorded.

Monic trinomials, in every degree

The root equation will eliminate the middle coefficient and control the polynomial on an entire segment, not just at its endpoints.

Theorem 2.1 (all-degree monic trinomials). Let 1 ≤𝑚 <𝑛1≤m<n and

𝑓(𝑧)=𝑧𝑛+𝑎𝑧𝑚+𝑏,f(z)=zn+azm+b,

with every zero in the open unit disc. For any zero 𝜁ζ, the entire segment [0,𝜁][0,ζ] lies in {|𝑓| <1}{|f|<1}. Distinct zeros 𝜁1,𝜁2ζ1,ζ2 are therefore joined by the broken line 𝜁1 →0 →𝜁2ζ1→0→ζ2 of length ‖𝜁1‖ +‖𝜁2‖ <2‖ζ1‖+‖ζ2‖<2 inside the open unit lemniscate.

𝑓(𝑡𝜁)=𝑏(1−𝑡𝑚)+𝜁𝑛(𝑡𝑛−𝑡𝑚).f(tζ)=b(1−tm)+ζn(tn−tm).

Vieta gives |𝑏| <1|b|<1. For 0 ≤𝑡 <10≤t<1, the weights 1 −𝑡𝑚1−tm and 𝑡𝑚 −𝑡𝑛tm−tn are nonnegative, so

|𝑓(𝑡𝜁)|≤|𝑏|(1−𝑡𝑚)+|𝜁|𝑛(𝑡𝑚−𝑡𝑛)<1−𝑡𝑛≤1.|f(tζ)|≤|b|(1−tm)+|ζ|n(tm−tn)<1−tn≤1.

Abel summation along a segment.

The same argument can be stated using partial sums. This explains both why trinomials work and what extra information a polynomial with more terms would require. For 𝑓(𝑧) =∑𝑛𝑘=0𝑎𝑘𝑧𝑘f(z)=∑k=0nakzk and 𝑓(𝜁) =0f(ζ)=0, put 𝑆𝑗 =∑𝑗𝑘=0𝑎𝑘𝜁𝑘Sj=∑k=0jakζk. Abel summation gives

𝑓(𝑡𝜁)=𝑛−1∑𝑗=0(𝑡𝑗−𝑡𝑗+1)𝑆𝑗.f(tζ)=∑j=0n−1(tj−tj+1)Sj.

For 0 ≤𝑡 <10≤t<1, the normalised value 𝑓(𝑡𝜁)/(1 −𝑡𝑛)f(tζ)/(1−tn) lies in the convex hull of 𝑆0,…,𝑆𝑛−1S0,…,Sn−1. A bound for each partial sum therefore gives a bound at every point of the segment. For a trinomial every partial sum equals either 𝑏b or −𝜁𝑛−ζn, both strictly inside the unit disc. This is a condition on the missing coefficients, not just on the root locations. For example, 𝑧𝑛 −𝑏zn−b with 0 <|𝑏| <10<|b|<1 is covered, whereas a general polynomial with four nonzero coefficients is not. The next example shows why the additional partial sums cannot simply be ignored.

Proposition 2.2 (failure of a prescribed radial segment). There exist 𝑟 ∈(0,1)r∈(0,1) for which every zero of

𝑓𝑟(𝑧)=𝑧6+15𝑟2𝑧4−15𝑟4𝑧2−𝑟6fr(z)=z6+15r2z4−15r4z2−r6

lies in the open unit disc, yet the radial spoke from the origin to the zero 𝑟r leaves {|𝑓𝑟| <1}{|fr|<1}.

Indeed, after 𝑧 =𝑟𝑤z=rw, the polynomial factors as 𝑟6(𝑤2 −1)(𝑤4 +65𝑤2 +1)r6(w2−1)(w4+65w2+1), so all six roots have modulus 𝑟r. However 𝑓𝑟(𝑟/2) = −(327/320)𝑟6fr(r/2)=−(327/320)r6. Any 𝑟r with 320/327 <𝑟6 <1320/327<r6<1 proves the assertion. This calculation rules out the segment [0,𝑟][0,r], not paths through a different root or a different joining point.

Low critical values and a uniform path bound

For 𝑡 ≥0t≥0, the set {|𝑓| ≤𝑡}{|f|≤t} grows from the roots as 𝑡t increases. For a squarefree polynomial, the first merger of two root components occurs at the smallest modulus of a critical value. We use the notation

𝐾𝑡={𝑧:|𝑓(𝑧)|≤𝑡},𝜇=min𝑓′(𝑐)=0|𝑓(𝑐)|,𝜌=𝜇1/𝑛.Kt={z:|f(z)|≤t},μ=minf′(c)=0|f(c)|,ρ=μ1/n.

Here 𝜇 >0μ>0 for a squarefree polynomial. A positive level 𝑡t is regular when no critical value has modulus 𝑡t. The quantity 𝜌ρ scales like a distance: for 𝑠 >0s>0, replacing 𝑓(𝑧)f(z) by 𝑠−𝑛𝑓(𝑠𝑧)s−nf(sz) divides 𝜌ρ by 𝑠s.

Theorem 3.1 (a small critical value). Let 𝑓f be squarefree and monic of degree 𝑛 ≥2n≥2, and let 𝜇μ be its least critical-value modulus. If 𝜇 ≤13/25μ≤13/25, then two distinct roots are joined inside {|𝑓| <1}{|f|<1} by a rectifiable curve of length strictly less than 22.

The condition 𝜇 ≤13/25μ≤13/25 is sufficient, not necessary. For 𝑓(𝑧) =𝑧𝑛 −𝑏f(z)=zn−b with 0 <|𝑏| <10<|b|<1, one has 𝜇 =|𝑏|μ=|b|, so this criterion covers |𝑏| ≤13/25|b|≤13/25 and excludes 13/25 <|𝑏| <113/25<|b|<1, even though the trinomial argument gives the required path throughout that family. Unlike that argument, the present criterion imposes no coefficient pattern and no root-location assumption. For example, (𝑧 −3)𝑛 −1/2(z−3)n−1/2 has 𝜇 =1/2μ=1/2 for every 𝑛 ≥2n≥2, yet all its roots satisfy |𝑧| >2|z|>2. The conclusion concerns |𝑓(𝑧)| <1|f(z)|<1, not containment in |𝑧| <1|z|<1.

Proof outline for the 13/2513/25 criterion.

The contradiction has two steps. Failure of a short path forces roots to be separated in a conformal disc. Packing then forces enough roots in a component to make its area grow faster than Pólya’s inequality allows. Section 3 of the companion record gives the complete analytic estimates and the rational comparison; we describe their dependence here.

Suppose no curve of length less than 22 joins two roots below level 11. For a regular level 𝜇 <𝑡 <1μ<t<1, let 𝐶𝑡Ct be the component of the open set {|𝑓| <𝑡}{|f|<t} containing a pair that first joins at level 𝜇μ, and put 𝑎 =Area⁡(𝐶𝑡)/𝜋a=Area⁡(Ct)/π. An inverse-map length estimate turns the failure assumption into pairwise hyperbolic separation of the roots in a Riemann disc. We use the normalisation 𝑑hyp(0,𝑠) =2artanh⁡𝑠dhyp(0,s)=2artanh⁡s. The map can be centred at a point ℎh on the two inverse arcs to the merging critical point whose intrinsic distance from every root is at least 11. Otherwise the disjoint intrinsic open balls of radius 11 about the roots would cover a connected set containing two roots. Here intrinsic distance means the infimum of lengths of curves in 𝐶𝑡Ct. In particular |𝑓(ℎ)| ≤𝜇|f(h)|≤μ.

If 𝑑1,…,𝑑𝑘d1,…,dk are the hyperbolic distances of the mapped roots from the origin, the Blaschke product identity gives

𝑘∑𝑗=1−log⁡tanh⁡(𝑑𝑗/2)=log⁡𝑡|𝑓(ℎ)|≥𝑥,𝑥=log⁡(𝑡/𝜇).∑j=1k−log⁡tanh⁡(dj/2)=log⁡t|f(h)|≥x,x=log⁡(t/μ).

Pairwise separation gives disjoint hyperbolic balls about the mapped roots. On each circle centred at the origin, their intersections occupy a total angle at most 2𝜋2π. Combining these simultaneous angular constraints with the displayed sum gives a lower bound for 𝑘k. The supplementary packing calculation states the finite inequality and explains why it must be certified at every permitted radial distance, not just on a sampled grid.

A second averaging argument converts the root count into area growth. Lift a common value ray from each root to the boundary and join adjacent endpoints by boundary arcs. Under the failure assumption, each of the 𝑘k resulting paths has length at least 22; their total length counts every lift twice and the boundary once. Coarea therefore gives a lower bound on area growth. The comparison combines the circle intersections with three other root-count bounds, derived in the companion, and exceeds Area⁡(𝐶𝑡) ≤𝜋𝑡2/𝑛Area⁡(Ct)≤πt2/n before 𝑡 =1t=1. The circle-intersection bound alone does not yield the stated cutoff.

The rational comparison reaches this contradiction when 𝜇 ≤13/25μ≤13/25. Its recorded stopping time also supports 𝜇 ≤529/1000μ≤529/1000; the supplement gives that calculation. No optimality of either cutoff is asserted.

Supplementary results

The main note ends with the preceding criterion and its scale-free corollary. The remaining results can be read independently of the trinomial argument. They distinguish control of a chosen component, control of critical values, and control of a prescribed curve. The companion record supplies the full area, separation and Poisson calculations at the locations specified below. The theorem numbering continues from the main note.

Intersect them with a hyperbolic circle of radius 𝑟 >0r>0 centred at the origin. Their angular measures add to at most 2𝜋2π. valid for every 𝑑 ≥2artanh⁡√1−𝑒−1/𝑎d≥2artanh⁡1−e−1/a, give

The Lean lemma for this last implication assumes the packing bound and boundedness; it does not cover the preceding hyperbolic geometry. Refinements using the number of roots, logarithmic capacity, or a range of levels during which a component still has two roots are given in research notes on the area argument and on components with two roots. Their length-22 conclusions under 𝜇 ≤1/2μ≤1/2 already follow from Theorem 3.1; their additional content is control of a specified component or a specified descent arc. A simple critical point need not be the unique point at the least critical level. The second note keeps these assumptions separate, since another merger can occur at the same level.

Critical proximity and straight-path obstructions

A critical point gives a different way to select two nearby roots, without assuming a sparse coefficient pattern. The logarithmic-derivative balance prevents one root from being arbitrarily closer to the critical point than all the others. This yields a bound on the sum of two distances. To turn that bound into a path theorem, both connecting segments would also have to stay inside the lemniscate; the examples below show why that extra step cannot be assumed.

Theorem 4.1 (a geometric-mean bound for distances to a critical point). Let 𝑛 ≥2n≥2, let 𝑧1,…,𝑧𝑛,𝑐 ∈ℂz1,…,zn,c∈C with 𝑐 ≠𝑧𝑘c≠zk for every 𝑘k, and suppose

𝑛∑𝑘=11𝑐−𝑧𝑘=0.∑k=1n1c−zk=0.

𝑟𝑛=𝑛∏𝑘=1|𝑐−𝑧𝑘|,rn=∏k=1n|c−zk|,

then there are distinct indices 𝑖,𝑗i,j such that

|𝑐−𝑧𝑖|+|𝑐−𝑧𝑗|≤2𝑟.|c−zi|+|c−zj|≤2r.

Uniqueness in the quintic rules out repairing that example by breaking a tie differently. The cubic excludes every direct root-to-root segment, not a curved path. Lean checks the whole proposition: the polynomials, the root locations, the critical point, uniqueness of the nearest root and both escapes.

Solved polynomial families

The following families allow containment to be proved along the whole path. Their assumptions are structural: rotational symmetry, two missing quintic coefficients, or collinearity. In each case the proof must do more than find nearby roots: it must bound the polynomial at every point of the chosen segments.

A cubic composed with a power map

The expression 𝑃((𝑧 −ℎ)𝑞)P((z−h)q) forces the roots to occur in regular 𝑞q-point sets about ℎh. This exact symmetry is the useful hypothesis; a generic perturbation of the coefficients destroys it. The point ℎh need not be the origin. Averaging over a complete set of rotated roots will show why the hypothesis on the roots of 𝑓f also controls the roots of the cubic 𝑃P.

Quintics with two missing coefficients

The coefficients of 𝑧3z3 and 𝑧2z2 must vanish in the coordinates used below. There is no separate smallness condition on the three remaining coefficients, but a general quintic is not covered. The two missing coefficients give the moment identities used to select two roots.

Sharp collinear roots

The complete all-degree collinear theorem appears in Section 14. It gives the sharp maximum modulus on a suitable root segment, as well as a bound on that segment’s length. Collinearity supplies a real ordering that is absent for a general complex root configuration. Lean checks the comparison of alternating values and the resulting Chebyshev bound.

Scope.

The proof above is also written out in a research note. Only the chosen critical point must be simple; other critical points may be multiple and their values may cluster outside the isolating disc. Existence of such an isolated value is not asserted.

Pendyala’s degree-four theorem [4] has no critical-value separation hypothesis. The present separation criterion applies in every degree 𝑛 ≥3n≥3 and supplies an explicit inverse-map length estimate.

Three limits of the sufficient conditions

These examples do not refute the root-to-root assertion. They show why particular sufficient conditions cannot be assumed for every polynomial. The rational calculations are checked in Lean, and a research note gives the ordinary arguments.

Proposition 7.1 (failure of two critical-value criteria to cover all polynomials). Let 𝑓(𝑧) =𝑧3 +(3/100)𝑧 −3/4f(z)=z3+(3/100)z−3/4. Every root lies in the open unit disc, both critical points are simple, the critical values lie on distinct positive rays, 𝜇 >13/25μ>13/25, and

The next example concerns successive mergers of sublevel components; the roots themselves do not move. The Newton value equation

The Newton equation is

𝑧′(𝑡)=−𝑓(𝑧(𝑡))𝑓′(𝑧(𝑡)).z′(t)=−f(z(t))f′(z(t)).

For an existing trajectory with nonzero initial value, the value moves inward on one positive ray. A zero value remains zero and has no argument. Thus a trajectory starting in {|𝑓| <1}{|f|<1} stays there at later times in its interval of existence. The equation neither constructs a global trajectory nor identifies a whole ray preimage with one flow line.

The time parameter matters when comparing this equation with gradient-flow theory. On {𝑓 ≠0}{f≠0}, the Euclidean gradient of 𝑢 = −log⁡|𝑓|u=−log⁡|f| is ∇𝑢 = −――――𝑓′/𝑓∇u=−f′/f―. Where 𝑓′ ≠0f′≠0, it is the positive multiple |𝑓′/𝑓|2( −𝑓/𝑓′)|f′/f|2(−f/f′) of the Newton field, so their nonstationary trajectories have the same orientation. At a simple critical point with nonzero value, the gradient extends smoothly as a hyperbolic saddle, whereas −𝑓/𝑓′−f/f′ is undefined. The exponential value equation uses Newton time; it is not unchanged by this reparametrisation.

Corollary 8.2 (ray separation). Let 𝑎 <𝑏a<b, let 𝑧 :[𝑎,𝑏] →ℂz:[a,b]→C be continuous, and suppose 𝑧z is differentiable on (𝑎,𝑏)(a,b) with 𝑓′(𝑧(𝑡)) ≠0f′(z(t))≠0 and 𝑧′(𝑡) = −𝑓(𝑧(𝑡))/𝑓′(𝑧(𝑡))z′(t)=−f(z(t))/f′(z(t)) there. Then

𝑓(𝑧(𝑏))=𝑒𝑎−𝑏𝑓(𝑧(𝑎)).f(z(b))=ea−bf(z(a)).

If the endpoint values are nonzero, they lie on the same positive ray. In particular, critical points whose values lie on distinct positive rays cannot be the endpoints of such a finite connection.

Apply the value equation inside (𝑎,𝑏)(a,b) and pass to the endpoints by continuity. This does not evaluate −𝑓/𝑓′−f/f′ at a critical endpoint. Lean checks the whole corollary, including the endpoint relation 𝑓(𝑧(𝑏)) =𝑒𝑎−𝑏𝑓(𝑧(𝑎))f(z(b))=ea−bf(z(a)), assuming only that 𝑓 ∘𝑧f∘z is continuous on [𝑎,𝑏][a,b]. Its last step, that values on distinct positive rays cannot satisfy this relation, is also a separate Lean lemma. Kozen and Stefánsson draw the same consequence for the Newtonian graph: under 𝑓f, every edge maps onto a segment of a ray through the origin whose endpoints are 00 or critical values . The endpoint behaviour of nonstationary maximal trajectories is classified there as well [6].

The Newtonian graph should not be confused with the quotient by whole trajectories. For 𝑓(𝑧) =𝑧2 −1/4f(z)=z2−1/4, the smooth-gradient flow on {log⁡2 ≤ −log⁡|𝑓| ≤log⁡8}{log⁡2≤−log⁡|f|≤log⁡8} has a real separatrix whose closure contains the saddle 00 as a different, stationary orbit. Its orbit class is not closed, so the orbit quotient is not Hausdorff, despite there being only one simple saddle and no saddle-to-saddle connection. A Hausdorff parameter space for cut strips must refer to the actual cut-open surface and its specified boundary identifications.

Arguments, not moduli

Two different nonzero numbers need not have different arguments: 11 and 22 have different moduli but lie on the same positive ray. By Corollary 8.2, different arguments of the endpoint values rule out a finite Newton connection. Distinct moduli, or merely distinct values, do not provide this obstruction.

For a polynomial whose critical values are already distinct, adding a constant translates all those values while leaving the critical points unchanged. The next formula identifies the translations to avoid. Its assumption 𝑎 ≠𝑏a≠b matters: a common translation can never separate two initially equal values.

Theorem 9.1 (ray-collision locus). Let 𝑎 ≠𝑏a≠b be complex. Every common translation 𝛽β for which 𝑎 +𝛽a+β and 𝑏 +𝛽b+β lie on the same positive ray has the form

𝛽=𝑟𝑎−𝑏1−𝑟,𝑟∈ℝ>0, 𝑟≠1.β=ra−b1−r,r∈R>0, r≠1.

Indeed, write 𝑏 +𝛽 =𝑟(𝑎 +𝛽)b+β=r(a+β) with 𝑟 >0r>0. Since 𝑎 ≠𝑏a≠b, one has 𝑟 ≠1r≠1, and solving for 𝛽β gives the displayed formula. Equivalently, 𝛽 = −𝑎 +(𝑎 −𝑏)/(1 −𝑟)β=−a+(a−b)/(1−r), so the forbidden translations lie on the real affine line through −𝑎−a and −𝑏−b.

Each pair of critical values contributes such a forbidden subset. These loci lie on finitely many real lines. Excluding those lines and the finitely many translations that make a value zero still leaves a point in every open disc. Accordingly, an arbitrarily small translation separates the arguments. Under an explicit margin, a small constant perturbation keeps the roots in the unit disc. For a constant shift there is also an elementary sharper estimate: if 𝑓(𝑧) =∏𝑛𝑗=1(𝑧 −𝑎𝑗)f(z)=∏j=1n(z−aj) has degree 𝑛 ≥1n≥1 and (𝑓 +𝛽)(𝑧) =0(f+β)(z)=0, then ∏𝑗|𝑧 −𝑎𝑗| =|𝛽|∏j|z−aj|=|β|, so min𝑗|𝑧 −𝑎𝑗| ≤|𝛽|1/𝑛minj|z−aj|≤|β|1/n. Thus max𝑗|𝑎𝑗| +|𝛽|1/𝑛 <1maxj|aj|+|β|1/n<1 suffices for root retention. This estimate does not assert a matching of labelled roots or control of a selected path. If a closed-level length bound holds on a dense class of polynomials, the fixed-degree lower semicontinuity in Section 17 extends that bound to its closure. Quantitative forward transport of a selected curve requires additional control, but is not a premise of that existence argument.

The distinct-value premise can be arranged first by a small linear perturbation: its local critical-value branches satisfy 𝑣′𝑗(𝜆) =𝑐𝑗(𝜆)vj′(λ)=cj(λ), so coincidences are isolated when the critical points are simple. Item 4 in Section 13 of the companion proves this qualitative statement, the subsequent choice of translation and root retention by Rouché’s theorem. It does not give quantitative control of a protected region or of the cost of transferring a selected path.

Why the proposed spanning-tree estimate fails

The estimate itself is false. Take the Cassini polynomial 𝑓𝑎(𝑧) =𝑧2 −𝑎2fa(z)=z2−a2 at 𝑎 =9/10a=9/10, with 2𝛼 = −log⁡𝑎2α=−log⁡a and 0 <𝑐 <𝛼/20<c<α/2. Its component contains the two roots at distance 9/59/5 and has a single nondegenerate saddle. Parametrising the level curves by 𝑧 = ±√𝑎2+𝑟𝑒𝑖𝜃z=±a2+reiθ, where 𝑟 =𝑒−𝑡r=e−t, and bounding the angular integral gives the upper majorant

4(√𝑎2+𝑎−𝑎)<41254(a2+a−a)<4125

for the right side of (5.1) before 𝜀ε, whereas every connected set containing both roots has length at least 9/59/5. Since 9/5 −41/25 =4/259/5−41/25=4/25, choosing a smaller positive 𝜀ε contradicts the assertion. Thus neither a different local saddle neighbourhood nor a perfect topological decomposition can recover the printed coefficient 1/(2𝜋)1/(2π). The exact finite inequality and the contradiction it gives for the proposed tree-length bound also have a Lean proof, in the repository’s research corpus, a library the checked build does not compile. The level-length majorant is an ordinary analytic calculation. The long record gives the parametrisation, angular bound and radial integral explicitly.

At an interior index-one critical point 𝑝p, the proof invokes a Morse chart

𝑢=𝑢(𝑝)+𝑥2−𝑦2u=u(p)+x2−y2

and replaces the saddle by a three-ended neighbourhood having one connected lower cross-section and two connected upper cross-sections. That local model is false as written. Because 𝑝 ∈𝑉p∈V and 𝑉V is open, a sufficiently small closed disc around 𝑝p lies entirely in 𝑉V. In that disc the full Morse chart has four sectors: two components of 𝑢 >𝑢(𝑝)u>u(p) and two components of 𝑢 <𝑢(𝑝)u<u(p). The level set {𝑢 =𝑢(𝑝)}{u=u(p)} is a lemniscate graph with a vertex of degree four at 𝑝p . A global component argument cannot delete one local sector from a disc already contained in 𝑉V.

This independently diagnoses a proof step, but the Cassini witness above also refutes the proposition’s statement. A different route might cut an adjoining regular annulus along a separatrix or regular flow arc before forming the block, retain a four-pronged saddle neighbourhood and change the assembly, or replace the local construction by the ray-cut decomposition proposed below. But no repair can retain (5.1); it must pay a positive attachment cost, select only one short pair instead of spanning every root, or use a different global metric inequality. The shorter descriptions of the same three-ended block do not repair the four-sector topology.

Within a component, distinct critical-value arguments exclude finite Newton connections between its saddles by Corollary 8.2. The companion’s inverse-sheet theorem supplies the corresponding component-wise construction. Its topology does not provide the missing length estimate or quantitative gluing.

Computational searches

The reported grid searches found candidate paths for sampled root configurations through degree ten. They supply no degree-wise upper bound. A raster path becomes a continuous certificate only after every connecting segment and its length have been enclosed. The sample counts, grid distances, and search parameters are retained in the long record. Useful diagnostics for further searches are clustered critical values, shrinking attachment windows, component mergers, and distance to the unit level.

The sharp Chebyshev bound for collinear roots

When all roots lie on one line, consecutive roots have an unambiguous order. Alternation against a Chebyshev polynomial then bounds the largest value on one of the intervening segments. The result covers every real-rooted polynomial after rotation and translation, but excludes any root set containing three noncollinear points. Put

𝐶𝑛=12𝑛−1cos𝑛⁡(𝜋/(2𝑛)).Cn=12n−1cosn⁡(π/(2n)).

|𝑓|≤𝐶𝑛(𝐷2)𝑛.|f|≤Cn(D2)n.

The constant is sharp: equality is attained by the affine images of the scaled Chebyshev root configuration with extreme roots at distance 𝐷D.

−1=𝑦1<⋯<𝑦𝑛=1,|𝑓|=𝑅𝑛|𝑞| on the root line.−1=y1<⋯<yn=1,|f|=Rn|q| on the root line.

𝑞∗(𝑥)=𝑇𝑛(𝑟𝑛𝑥)2𝑛−1𝑟𝑛𝑛.q∗(x)=Tn(rnx)2n−1rnn.

Each maximum is attained in the interior, since 𝑞q vanishes at the endpoints and not in the gap. Its signs at the 𝑛 −1n−1 chosen points alternate because the roots are simple. If every gap maximum exceeded 𝐶𝑛Cn, then ℎ =𝑞 −𝑞∗h=q−q∗ would have those same nonzero signs at the 𝑐𝑖ci. The intermediate value theorem would give 𝑛 −2n−2 distinct zeros between consecutive chosen points, in addition to the zeros at −1−1 and 11. For sharpness take the roots of 𝑞∗q∗, namely

cos⁡((2𝑘−1)𝜋/(2𝑛))𝑟𝑛,1≤𝑘≤𝑛.cos⁡((2k−1)π/(2n))rn,1≤k≤n.

The fourth-power refinement.

The quadratic exponent is not the limit of this Poisson argument. In the same notation, put 𝐻 =𝑔2 =1 +∑𝜈≥1𝑏𝜈𝑧𝜈H=g2=1+∑ν≥1bνzν. This choice makes |𝐻|2 =𝐺4|H|2=G4, while the kernel identity becomes 𝑃 =1 −ℜ(𝜁𝐻′/𝐻)P=1−ℜ(ζH′/H). For interior points the preceding calculation gives

∑𝑗𝑤𝑗𝐺(𝑐𝑗)4≤∫|𝐻|2𝑃𝑑𝑚=1−∑𝜈≥1(𝜈−1)|𝑏𝜈|2≤1.∑jwjG(cj)4≤∫|H|2Pdm=1−∑ν≥1(ν−1)|bν|2≤1.

All coefficient weights are nonnegative, including the zero weight at 𝜈 =1ν=1. The same radial contraction, applied first to finite coefficient sums, proves the inequality for closed-disc points. This is the 𝑝 =4p=4 case of the ordinary power-parameter Poisson identity. The long record proves its extension under vanishing complex power sums and handles equality at this endpoint. Lean does not check this refinement.

Relation to classical critical-value products.

For a monic polynomial with all zeros in the unit disc, Dubinin proves the sharp geometric-mean inequality (∏𝑛−1𝑗=1|𝑓(𝑐𝑗)|)1/(𝑛−1) ≤1(∏j=1n−1|f(cj)|)1/(n−1)≤1. The proof uses the resultant identity (9), the maximum-modulus principle and Schur’s unit-circle Vandermonde inequality, not the dissymmetrisation argument of his Theorem 1. The positive-moment inequality below implies that product bound by AM–GM. For a list with at least two entries, a product bound alone does not control a positive moment; in degree two there is only one critical value, so the two bounds are equivalent. This comparison identifies an antecedent, not a priority claim for the stronger moment statement.

Theorem 15.2 (critical-value mean in every degree). Let 𝑓f be monic of degree 𝑛 ≥2n≥2, with roots in a closed disc of radius 𝑅R, and let 𝑐1,…,𝑐𝑛−1c1,…,cn−1 be its critical points with multiplicity. Then

𝑛−1∑𝑗=1|𝑓(𝑐𝑗)|2/(𝑛−1)≤(𝑛−1)𝑅2𝑛/(𝑛−1).∑j=1n−1|f(cj)|2/(n−1)≤(n−1)R2n/(n−1).

In particular, ∑𝑗|𝑓(𝑐𝑗)|1/𝑛 ≤(𝑛 −1)𝑅∑j|f(cj)|1/n≤(n−1)R in every degree.

|𝑓(𝑐𝑗)|≤∏𝑘|1−―――𝑐𝑘𝑐𝑗|.|f(cj)|≤∏k|1−ck―cj|.

The reflected-derivative lemma in Section 8 of the companion supplies the displayed modulus comparison and the contraction argument explicitly. ◻

The same pointwise comparison transfers the fourth-power Poisson bound. With 𝑚 =𝑛 −1m=n−1 and equal weights, on the unit disc

1𝑚∑𝑗|𝑓(𝑐𝑗)|4/𝑚≤1𝑚∑𝑗𝐺(𝑐𝑗)4≤1.1m∑j|f(cj)|4/m≤1m∑jG(cj)4≤1.

If a zero is fixed at the disc centre, Dubinin’s Theorem 3 gives the sharper product estimate (∏𝑗|𝑓(𝑐𝑗)|)1/(𝑛−1) ≤(𝑛 −1)(|𝑓′(0)|2/𝑛𝑛)1/(𝑛−1)(∏j|f(cj)|)1/(n−1)≤(n−1)(|f′(0)|2/nn)1/(n−1) in the unit-disc normalisation. Dubinin explicitly records the preceding contribution of Tischler [20]. Neither the product estimate nor its equality family settles the marked-zero positive-moment question in the research addendum .

For a fixed containing disc ――𝐷(ℎ,𝑅)D―(h,R) with 𝑅 >0R>0, the equality cases in Theorem 15.2 are exactly 𝑓(𝑧) =(𝑧 −ℎ)𝑛 −𝜆f(z)=(z−h)n−λ with |𝜆| =𝑅𝑛|λ|=Rn. Indeed, after normalising this disc, equality in the critical-value bound forces equality in the equal-weight Poisson inequality. All critical points are then 00, so 𝑓′ =𝑛𝑧𝑛−1f′=nzn−1 and 𝑓 =𝑧𝑛 −𝜆f=zn−λ; equality forces |𝜆| =1|λ|=1. Scaling back gives the stated family. The same argument covers equality in the lower-exponent consequence, since equality in the chain of power-mean bounds forces equality in the quadratic bound. This equality classification is an ordinary consequence of the proof. A bound on the critical values alone gives neither a curve nor a length estimate.

A nonlinear integral for component mergers

Consider a component containing 𝑘k roots that later joins a larger component as the level of |𝑓||f| increases. If 𝑟 ∈(0,1]r∈(0,1] is the ratio of these two merger scales, one logarithmic contribution assigned to each of its roots is 𝑘−1log⁡(1/𝑟)k−1log⁡(1/r). An earlier length estimate instead involves the integral

𝐼𝑘(𝑟)=∫1𝑟𝑑𝑞𝑞log⁡((1+𝑞2/𝑘)/(1−𝑞2/𝑘)).Ik(r)=∫r1dqqlog⁡((1+q2/k)/(1−q2/k)).

For nearby merger scales, 𝑟r is close to 11. The integral is then much smaller than 𝑘−1log⁡(1/𝑟)k−1log⁡(1/r). The following change of variables proves that no fixed positive multiple of this logarithmic contribution is a uniform lower bound.

Theorem 16.1 (the relation between two merger-scale integrals). Define

Φ(𝑥)=∫𝑥0𝑑𝑡log⁡(coth⁡𝑡)(𝑥≥0).Φ(x)=∫0xdtlog⁡(coth⁡t)(x≥0).

𝐼𝑘(𝑟)=𝑘Φ(𝑥).(O1)(O1)Ik(r)=kΦ(x).

The function ΦΦ is increasing and strictly convex on (0,∞)(0,∞), and

Consequently, for every fixed 𝑘 ≥1k≥1 and every 𝑐 >0c>0, some 0 <𝑟 <10<r<1 satisfies

𝐼𝑘(𝑟)<𝑐1𝑘log⁡1𝑟.(O3)(O3)Ik(r)<c1klog⁡1r.

Proof. Set 𝑞 =𝑒−𝑘𝑡q=e−kt. Then 𝑑𝑞/𝑞 = −𝑘 𝑑𝑡dq/q=−kdt, the endpoints 𝑞 =1,𝑟q=1,r become 𝑡 =0,𝑥t=0,x, and

1+𝑒−2𝑡1−𝑒−2𝑡=coth⁡𝑡,1+e−2t1−e−2t=coth⁡t,

which proves (O1). Since coth⁡𝑡coth⁡t, and hence log⁡(coth⁡𝑡)log⁡(coth⁡t), is strictly decreasing, the positive integrand 1/log⁡(coth⁡𝑡)1/log⁡(coth⁡t) is strictly increasing. This proves monotonicity and strict convexity. Moreover

0≤Φ(𝑥)𝑥≤1log⁡(coth⁡𝑥)⟶0,0≤Φ(x)x≤1log⁡(coth⁡x)⟶0,

which gives (O2); taking 𝑟 =𝑒−𝑘𝑥r=e−kx gives (O3). ◻

As 𝑟r approaches 11, two successive merger scales approach each other. The integral can then be arbitrarily small relative to the logarithmic contribution, even for fixed 𝑘k. Any estimate along a chain of mergers must retain this nonlinear dependence. Related weighted Jensen estimates and a lemma selecting two roots with small total logarithmic contribution are given in a research note. Those inequalities do not by themselves construct pieces of a contained path that meet one another.

Fixed-degree limits and the earlier approach

Fix 𝑛 ≥2n≥2, and let K𝑛Kn be the compact coefficient class of monic degree-𝑛n polynomials with roots in the closed unit disc. Define

Λ(𝑓)=inf𝛾length⁡(𝛾),Λ(f)=infγlength⁡(γ),

where 𝛾 ⊂{|𝑓| ≤1}γ⊂{|f|≤1} joins two different listed root occurrences. A repeated root permits a constant curve; an empty set of competitors has infimum +∞+∞.

Passing a length bound to a limit.

The function ΛΛ is lower semicontinuous, and a finite infimum is attained. Indeed, near-minimising curves of bounded length can be parametrised on [0,1][0,1] with a common Lipschitz bound. Arzelà–Ascoli, convergence of root multisets and lower semicontinuity of length give a contained limiting curve, even if the two endpoint occurrences coalesce. The fixed-degree limits subsection of the companion gives the full argument.

Thus a bound Λ ≤2Λ≤2 on a dense class would extend to its closure. For an open-disc polynomial, rescaling a containing radius 𝑅 <1R<1 would give length at most 2𝑅 <22R<2 in {|𝑓| ≤𝑅𝑛} ⊂{|𝑓| <1}{|f|≤Rn}⊂{|f|<1}. The binomial 𝑧𝑛 −1zn−1 has Λ =2Λ=2: its root sectors meet only at zero, and the radial paths attain this length. These facts explain the historical reduction. They also show that the bound fails in degree seven: if 𝑅 <1R<1 exceeds the root moduli of the polynomial 𝑓f of ani in Section 1, then 𝑅−7𝑓(𝑅𝑧)R−7f(Rz) lies in K7K7 and has Λ >2Λ>2, because a contained curve of length at most 22 would rescale to a curve in {|𝑓| <1}{|f|<1} of length below 22, whose image has one-dimensional Hausdorff measure below 22. The reduction remains available on separately specified polynomial classes.

The particular curves used in the earlier approach.

For polynomials whose critical points are simple and whose critical values are nonzero, with pairwise distinct arguments and moduli, cutting the value plane along critical rays gives the finite inverse-sheet construction of a research note. The underlying inverse-sheet construction is classical: Dubinin [16] cuts outward from the critical values and describes the resulting sheet adjacency tree; [22] uses a related network in a capacity argument. The latter assumes critical values bounded by one and controls logarithmic capacity, not Euclidean length. Here the task is to specify admissible descent arcs and estimate their metric cost. Let 𝐿𝑓(𝑐)Lf(c) be the length of the curve formed by the two inverse lifts of [0,𝑓(𝑐)][0,f(c)] meeting at a critical point 𝑐c. This length is finite under the stated hypotheses: the inverse derivative has an integrable inverse-square-root singularity at the simple critical endpoint and is regular at the root endpoint. Its halves are Newton-flow trajectories from 𝑐c to roots, that is, edges of the Newtonian graph [6]. These curves lie in {|𝑓| ≤1}{|f|≤1} precisely when |𝑓(𝑐)| ≤1|f(c)|≤1. A sufficient length bound is

min𝑓′(𝑐)=0|𝑓(𝑐)|≤1𝐿𝑓(𝑐)≤2.minf′(c)=0|f(c)|≤1Lf(c)≤2.

Since ΛΛ minimises over all curves, the minimum over these inverse-ray curves is an upper bound for ΛΛ. Equality between the two minimisations is not assumed. In a unit-sublevel component, the sheets and tree use only that component’s critical points; equal values in another component do not invalidate this local construction. These ordinary topological steps are not formalised here and supply no length estimate.

The attachment obstruction is quantitative.

For 𝑓(𝑧) =𝑧𝑛 −𝑟𝑛f(z)=zn−rn with 𝑟 >0r>0, consider the value ray {𝑠𝑒𝑖𝜃 :𝑠 ≥0}{seiθ:s≥0}. Along any of its inverse lifts, |𝑧|𝑛 =|𝑟𝑛 +𝑠𝑒𝑖𝜃||z|n=|rn+seiθ|. The minimum over 𝑠 ≥0s≥0 is 𝑟𝑛rn when cos⁡𝜃 ≥0cos⁡θ≥0, and 𝑟𝑛|sin⁡𝜃|rn|sin⁡θ| otherwise. Thus a lift meets 𝐵(0,𝜀)B(0,ε), with 0 <𝜀 <𝑟0<ε<r, precisely when

cos⁡𝜃<0,|sin⁡𝜃|<(𝜀/𝑟)𝑛.cos⁡θ<0,|sin⁡θ|<(ε/r)n.

The permitted directions therefore form an interval about 𝜋π of width 2arcsin⁡((𝜀/𝑟)𝑛)2arcsin⁡((ε/r)n). A bound averaged over all directions need not hold on this shrinking interval. An argument that must join its paths near the critical point needs control there, or must leave the joining point free. The binomial itself is solved by radial segments.

Which information is insufficient.

The sextic of Proposition 2.2 excludes automatic control of every prescribed root-to-origin segment once further partial sums occur. The exact Cassini example in Section 11 excludes the historical global tree-length estimate even after the local saddle model is corrected. The examples in Section 7 show that the least critical modulus and the separation test with radius 22 do not cover all polynomials, and that the number of roots at the first merger does not control capacity after subsequent mergers. The critical-value inequalities bound sums of powers of the moduli; they do not choose inverse branches that join to form the required path. A research note on powers of Blaschke products gives fixed-degree tests of these limitations and separate asymptotic results for the shortest contained path. The family, certificate scope, centroid restriction and two distinct parameter regimes are given in the Blaschke-product subsection of the companion, after the compactness functional is defined. Neither a failed sufficient condition nor a fixed-degree certificate settles an asymptotic path estimate.

The earlier note gives a near-regular-pentagon family for which all origin segments escape [21]. The long record gives the two-scale proof along the five segments, including the open-disc contraction. The addendum reports a stronger failure for every critical joining point, but its proof is not available. Failure at the origin, which is not a critical point of this family, does not establish that stronger assertion. Neither straight-segment claim excludes a different vertex, curved inverse-ray arms or an arbitrary contained connector.

Outside the cases covered by the structural results, the separation criterion and the recorded certificate consequence 𝜇 ≤529/1000μ≤529/1000, these arguments give no general conclusion. In particular, exceeding a sufficient cutoff is not evidence for or against the unrestricted assertion. On any class where a stronger positive result is sought, the same selected pair must satisfy both containment and a length estimate. The long record gives the examples showing why root distances and critical-value means do not ensure this.

Sources and adjacent results

The original root-to-root problem is [2]. Pendyala’s degree-four theorem is directly comparable. Erdős Problem #1120, treated by Pendyala [5], asks for a path from 00 to the unit circle inside {|𝑧| ≤1, |𝑓(𝑧)| ≤1}{|z|≤1, |f(z)|≤1}. Its admissible region includes the unit-disc restriction, and its endpoints are not a chosen pair of roots. It does not imply the root-pair conclusion. The exact Cassini obstruction in Section 11 concerns the metric assertion of [3]. Eremenko and Hayman prove the global boundary estimate length⁡{𝑧 :|𝑝(𝑧)| =1} <9.173deg⁡𝑝length⁡{z:|p(z)|=1}<9.173deg⁡p and show that an extremal level set is connected . Their metric is the total length of a level curve, so this does not supply the short internal root-to-root connector asked for here.

The Newton value identity of Section 8 is a lemma of Shub, Tischler and Williams, and the ray-segment description of Newton-flow edges belongs to their Newtonian graph; we use both in the form recorded by Kozen and Stefánsson [6]. The area arguments use Pólya’s inequality and the area–capacity inequality in the formulations [7]; the square-root uniformisation uses the component-wise Riemann–Hurwitz count in the proof of [8]. Existence of a contained root segment for collinear zeros already follows from [2]; Section 14 adds the sharp constant. Crane’s Smale mean-value argument [17] combines inverse branches, radial slits and capacity, but concerns a derivative-normalised mean-value ratio rather than our absolute monic critical values. Dubinin’s four-point theorem [18] assumes a bound on all critical values and concerns distortion; its normalisation does not supply our root-disc moment or path estimate. Kuznetsova and Tkachev [19] study length functions on regular lemniscate levels. Their log-convexity is useful context, not a uniform one-root perimeter bound at a critical endpoint. The long record gives further source comparisons and the history of the withdrawn argument. No uniqueness or priority claim is inferred from this comparison.
